snippet.title: The Lies You Tell Yourself
snippet.description:
Most creatives think storytelling is something you do for an audience. 

But the most powerful story you'll ever tell is the one only you hear.

Closing out his talk at FOMO in Bucharest,  ⁨@ChrisDo⁩   shares the story he told himself for years and the moment he decided to rewrite it. 

You'll learn the simple structure that makes people care about your story, and why that story almost always starts in your past. 

Then you'll learn how to use the same skill on yourself: spot the old story that's holding you back, write a new one, and stop waiting for permission to change. 

In this episode:
● You want to tell stories that make people care.
● You say "I can't" before you've even tried.
● You've made peace with an old story about who you are.
● You're waiting for someone's permission to change.

snippet.title: How to Stand Out When Everyone Sells the Same Thing
snippet.description:
🚨Watch the Full Masterclass here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkcW4VqJqbw

If customers cannot tell you apart from your competitors, more marketing will not fix your brand positioning.

Most businesses fail because they play it safe and try to appeal to everyone. In this audit, we analyze two rival candle makers who appear identical on paper. You will see how one company can stand out and capture market share without spending a single extra dollar on advertising. We look at the specific brand attribute slider used to force clear decisions and differentiate your company in a crowded market.

Learn how to craft a repeatable brand story that resonates with your customers so they do the marketing for you. By refining your business branding, you move away from the middle ground where brands go to die and start building a distinct identity that competitors cannot easily copy. Mastering this marketing strategy is essential for any creative business owner looking to stop guessing and start growing.

Subscribe for more business strategy breakdowns, and tell us your biggest branding struggle below.
In this episode:
● Your product is as good as your competitor's, but customers can't tell you apart.
● Someone asks where your brand stands, and you say "kind of in the middle."
● Your best story lives on Instagram, not on the product people actually pick up.
● You depend on staff to explain your brand, and not all of them can.
● You've wondered whether a more impressive, less true story would sell better.

snippet.title: How To Get A Client To Reveal Their Real Budget
snippet.description:
🚨 You're watching a slice of the full masterclass. Watch the FOMO series:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zmENYq6PJ-A

Most people wait for the client to bring up money first — and lose the negotiation before it even starts.

Live on stage at the FOMO Festival of Modern Owners in Bucharest, @ChrisDo runs unscripted pricing role-plays with audience members — pulling them into real client calls to test how they handle a vague budget, a lowball offer, or a client who won't commit.

Through these live exercises, Chris breaks down price anchoring — why the first person to name a number controls the negotiation — along with how to bring up cost early, qualify or disqualify a client fast, and get someone to tell you their real budget instead of a guess.

In this episode:
● You struggle to bring up price without feeling awkward.
● You're not sure what to do when a client won't share their budget.
● You want to disqualify bad-fit clients faster instead of wasting time.
● You avoid negotiating in person and hide behind emails or DMs.
● You wonder how to get a client to tell you their real budget.
● You want to feel confident stating your price first.

snippet.description:
You don't need more marketing to get more clients. You need proof — told as a story — that makes them say yes.

Through these live sessions, Chris breaks down the imagination gap — why explaining your value harder never closes a sale, and proof does — along with how to package that proof into a story that actually gets felt, and how to stop guessing at who you're even trying to reach by narrowing down to one ideal client in minutes.

In this episode:
● You've done great work but still hear "let me think about it."
● You struggle to prove your value without over-explaining it.
● You want your portfolio or content to actually convert, not just look good.
● You don't know how to structure a story so people feel it, not just see it.
● You're stuck trying to serve too many types of clients.
● You want a fast way to define your one ideal client instead of guessing.

snippet.title: The Personal Branding Lesson Nobody Teaches
snippet.description:
Your personal brand isn't generic because of your strategy. It's generic because you're still building it to win over a business partner, a client, or a troll who was never going to approve anyway.

At the FOMO Festival Q&A, @ChrisDo answers a question about building a personal brand alongside a business partner with one diagnostic instead: who's your number one fan, and who's your number one troll?

You'll learn why playing it safe is what makes a brand generic, how to tell the difference between feedback worth keeping and feedback you're only listening to out of fear, and why refusing to let a business partner, a client, or a critic cast the deciding vote is what makes a brand actually yours.

In this episode:
● You shape your content around people who were never going to approve of you anyway.
● You can't tell if feedback should change your brand or if you're just afraid to ignore it.
● You water down your point of view so you don't rock the boat.
● Your brand looks like everyone else's because it's built to avoid criticism, not express a point of view.
● You want a personal brand people remember, not one that blends in.

Stop chasing others and start focusing on your own self worth in relationships. Learn why being the prize changes every dynamic.

Many people lose their power because they view their partner as the prize. This video breaks down why that mindset creates an uneven playing field and how to shift your perspective to regain control in your interactions. If you constantly feel like you are losing or chasing, you are likely negotiating from a position of weakness.

This advice is for anyone struggling with dating mindset issues or feeling undervalued in their connections. By adopting a high value mindset, you stop giving the other person an ally in the negotiation against yourself. We explore the psychology behind why you must prioritize your own value to foster healthier, more balanced dynamics.

Subscribe for weekly relationship advice breakdowns, and comment below: do you find it difficult to maintain your boundaries when you really like someone?

Niching down feels wrong because it forces you to say no to most of the market. But that’s exactly why it works.

In this live business coaching session, we break down why most entrepreneurs, creators, consultants, and service providers struggle to pick a niche — and why trying to serve everyone usually means serving no one. If you’ve ever felt stuck choosing your ideal client, defining your ICP, or deciding who your business is really for, this conversation will help you see niching down in a much simpler way.

You’ll learn why specialization creates clarity, why generalists often struggle to stand out, and how narrowing your audience can actually make your offer stronger. We also talk about “the dip” — the painful stage where most people quit right before things start working — and why persistence matters when building a business, personal brand, or content strategy. The transcript directly centers on specialization, the idea that serving too many people leads to serving no one, and the importance of pushing through the hard stage before growth happens.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why niching down feels scary but creates more opportunity
How to stop being too broad with your business
Why specialization beats being a generalist
How to define your ideal client profile, or ICP
Why most people quit before they get results
How to use constraints to choose a better niche
Why “hard” markets often have less competition

If you’re a business owner, creative entrepreneur, consultant, coach, agency owner, designer, or personal brand trying to figure out your niche, this video will help you get clearer about who you serve and why that clarity matters.

The big lesson: niching down is not about limiting your potential. It’s about making your message, offer, and business easier for the right people to understand.

snippet.title: The Psychology of Making People Buy
snippet.description:
Most brands fight for attention by competing on price, features, and quality.

But cult brands create demand differently.

In this video, @ChrisDo  breaks down the marketing psychology behind brands like Liquid Death, Dude Wipes, Method Soap, Honda motorcycles, and Better Call Saul’s infamous phone-selling scene.

The lesson is simple: people don’t just buy products. They buy meaning, identity, status, fear, privacy, belonging, and desire.

This is the psychology of making people buy — not through manipulation, but through positioning.

You’ll learn how smart brands create their own lane, escape the red ocean of competition, and make ordinary products feel impossible to ignore. From water in a can to soap in a beautiful bottle to a motorcycle category nobody knew they wanted, these examples reveal how demand is created before the sale ever happens.

If you sell a service, build a brand, run a business, or create content, this will change how you think about marketing.

In this episode:
• How brands create demand instead of chasing customers
• The psychology behind Liquid Death, Dude Wipes, Method Soap, and Honda
• What Better Call Saul teaches us about positioning
• How to sell meaning, not just features
• The ethical line between persuasion and manipulation
• How to apply these marketing lessons to your own business

• Why virality is often a trap, not a strategy
• The emotional cost of chasing attention online

In this video, Chris Do breaks down the connection between Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, brand loyalty, and how emotional drivers like identity, community, and personal growth influence what we buy.
